werk/joe-cocker-stingray.text:
Stingray is Joe Cocker's sixth studio album, released in 1976. As before, it consists mostly of covers. Born Thru Indifference, written with Richard Tee, is the only original song. Bob Dylan remains a favourite source, with two of his songs on the record: The Man in Me and Catfish. Dylan's own version of Catfish would not appear until 1991.

Rob Fraboni produced the album, which was partly recorded at Dynamic Sound Studios in Kingston, Jamaica. Richard Tee directs the arrangements, and the band includes Steve Gadd on drums and Cornell Dupree and Eric Gale on guitar, while Eric Clapton plays a guitar solo on Worrier. Peter Tosh contributed to the arrangements of The Man in Me. The New Rolling Stone Record Guide saw signs of renewal, thanks in part to the band Stuff and the above-average material.
werk/joe-cocker-stingray.listen: Listen to A Song for You and notice how Cocker sings this long closing track and what the band does around him.

werk/joe-cocker-with-a-little-help-from-.text:
This debut album was released in April 1969, with producer Denny Cordell behind the desk. Cordell brought together a remarkable cast: American soul singers such as Merry Clayton and Madeline Bell alongside well-known British rock musicians, among them Jimmy Page, Steve Winwood and Albert Lee. Joe Cocker sings mostly other people's songs, from Bob Dylan to Traffic and The Beatles, and makes them entirely his own. His raw, soulful voice, influenced by Ray Charles, takes centre stage. A light little song like Bye Bye Blackbird becomes a lament full of longing, and the title song, originally by the Beatles, grows into something quite different from the original.

The press was positive. Rolling Stone called it a triumph, and Robert Christgau described it as the greatest achievement in rock interpretation to date. AllMusic later praised above all the surprising arrangements. The album went gold in the United States.
werk/joe-cocker-with-a-little-help-from-.listen: Listen to With a Little Help from My Friends and notice how Cocker transforms the Beatles song: can you hear how the light-footed tune becomes a pleading story?

werk/joe-farrell-penny-arcade.text:
Penny Arcade is a jazz album released on CTI Records. It was recorded in October 1973 at Van Gelder Studio, with Rudy Van Gelder as engineer and Creed Taylor as producer. Joe Farrell plays tenor saxophone, soprano saxophone, flute and piccolo, and he is surrounded by a strong group: Herbie Hancock on piano, Joe Beck on guitar, Steve Gadd on drums, Herb Bushler on bass and Don Alias on congas. The title piece is by Joe Beck, Too High is by Stevie Wonder, and the saxophonist wrote the other three pieces himself.

DownBeat found him a great player but only an average composer. The reviewer praised the fluid, melodic saxophone playing in Geo Blue and Hancock's acoustic piano in Cloud Cream.
werk/joe-farrell-penny-arcade.listen: In Geo Blue, listen to the saxophone and notice how fluid and melodic the lines sound.

werk/joe-henderson-in-n-out.text:
In 'n Out is the third album by jazz saxophonist Joe Henderson, released on the Blue Note label. It was recorded on 10 April 1964. The tenor saxophonist plays with trumpeter Kenny Dorham, pianist McCoy Tyner, bassist Richard Davis and drummer Elvin Jones. He wrote most of the pieces himself; Short Story and Brown's Town are by Dorham. The opening track In 'N Out runs to well over ten minutes and is the longest piece on the record.

AllMusic reviewer Scott Yanow writes that the leader can make a routine bop pattern sound complicated and the most complicated free improvisation sound logical. In his view the music still sounds fresh after thirty years. The Penguin Guide to Jazz observes that the temperature seems lower than on the saxophonist's other Blue Note records, but calls it fascinating, deep music.
werk/joe-henderson-in-n-out.listen: Listen to In 'n Out and try to follow how trumpet and tenor saxophone take turns leading in this long opening piece.

werk/joe-henderson-inner-urge.text:
Inner Urge was recorded on 30 November 1964 at Van Gelder's studio in Englewood Cliffs and released on Blue Note in 1966. It is the fourth record Joe Henderson made as a leader. He played with pianist McCoy Tyner and drummer Elvin Jones, who were both in John Coltrane's quartet at the time, and with bassist Bob Cranshaw.

The title song, now a jazz standard, is about the anger and frustration of life in New York, according to Henderson. Isotope is a tribute to Thelonious Monk and his musical humour. El Barrio refers to his bond with Spanish music. The critic Norman Weinstein calls it his most emotionally urgent album, and The Penguin Guide to Jazz describes the music as dark and intense. Guitarist Alex Skolnick counts the record among his favourites.
werk/joe-henderson-inner-urge.listen: Listen to Inner Urge, the longest track, and notice the intense, dark atmosphere the band creates here.

werk/joe-henderson-our-thing.text:
Our Thing is Joe Henderson's second record for Blue Note. He plays tenor saxophone alongside trumpeter Kenny Dorham, pianist Andrew Hill, drummer Pete La Roca and bassist Eddie Khan. The pieces are by Henderson himself and by Dorham: Teeter Totter and Our Thing are by Henderson, Pedro's Time, Back Road and Escapade by Dorham. Alfred Lion produced, Rudy Van Gelder was the engineer and Reid Miles designed the cover.

Scott Yanow gave the album four and a half stars in his review for AllMusic. He wrote that even at this early stage Henderson showed he had the potential to become a great tenor saxophonist. The CD reissue includes an extra version of Teeter Totter, an alternate take that is shorter than the version on the original record.
werk/joe-henderson-our-thing.listen: Listen to Pedro's Time, the longest track on the record, and notice Henderson's tenor saxophone alongside Dorham's trumpet.

werk/joe-henderson-page-one.text:
Page One is the debut album of tenor saxophonist Joe Henderson, recorded and released in 1963 by Blue Note Records. He plays in a quintet with trumpeter Kenny Dorham, pianist McCoy Tyner, bassist Butch Warren and drummer Pete La Roca. The pieces were written by the leader or by Dorham. Tyner is credited on the cover as ETC., because he was then under contract to the rival Impulse! Records.

Two pieces became jazz standards: Recorda Me by the saxophonist and Blue Bossa by Dorham. AllMusic calls it an exceptionally strong and historic record, and All About Jazz still counts it among his most acclaimed albums. PopMatters feels it has the cautious air of a leader's first session.
werk/joe-henderson-page-one.listen: Listen to Blue Bossa, which became a jazz standard, and notice the difference in tone between the trumpet and the tenor saxophone.

werk/joe-walsh-barnstorm.text:
Barnstorm was released in October 1972 on ABC-Dunhill Records and is regarded as guitarist Joe Walsh's first solo album, although it was also the debut of the band Barnstorm. He had just left the James Gang. It was the first album to be recorded at Caribou Ranch in Colorado.

He largely left the hard rock of the James Gang behind for a more folk-like, acoustic sound, influenced by James Taylor and Crosby, Stills and Nash. He experimented with an ARP Odyssey synthesizer, slide guitar and a guitar run through a Leslie speaker for an organ-like tone. The only real hard rock track, Turn To Stone, became the best known. The album was only moderately successful on release but grew into a cult favourite. AllMusic called Birdcall Morning one of the most beautiful rock love songs of the early seventies.
werk/joe-walsh-barnstorm.listen: Listen to Birdcall Morning and notice the interplay of acoustic and electric guitars.

werk/joe-walsh-but-seriously-folks.text:
In mid-1978 But Seriously, Folks... was released on the Asylum label, the fourth studio album by the American singer and guitarist. He had by then been in the Eagles for two years, and all the other members of that band play on the record. You also hear keyboardist Jay Ferguson, drummer Joe Vitale from his former band Barnstorm and bassist Willie Weeks. Bill Szymczyk produced the album, which was recorded at Bayshore Studios in Florida.

The best-known song is the satirical Life's Been Good. The album version runs to well over eight minutes; for the single it was cut down to 4:35. It became his biggest solo hit. Critics were divided about the album as a whole: one thought most of the songs fell short, another called it his most considered and melodic record, a reflective song cycle.
werk/joe-walsh-but-seriously-folks.listen: Listen to Life's Been Good in the long album version. Notice how the satire unfolds over more than eight minutes and what the short single version must have left out.

werk/joe-walsh-so-what.text:
At the end of 1974 So What was released on ABC-Dunhill Records, the third studio album by the American singer and multi-instrumentalist. He had put off its release for a long time, because after six or seven records he wanted to take a big step forward in singing, playing and maturity. Producer Bill Szymczyk worked on the result. On a few tracks Don Henley, Glenn Frey and Randy Meisner of the Eagles sing along, a good year and a half before he would join that band.

The album contains solid hard rock, such as Welcome To the Club and a new version of Turn To Stone, and more reflective songs such as Help Me Thru the Night. He wrote Song For Emma in memory of his young daughter, who had been killed in a car accident that spring. Later critics praised above all the guitar solos and the classic rock sound.
werk/joe-walsh-so-what.listen: Listen to Song For Emma and remember that this track is a memory of his daughter, who had died. Notice how different the mood is from the hard rock of Welcome To the Club.

werk/joe-walsh-the-smoker-you-drink-the-.text:
The Smoker You Drink, the Player You Get, from 1973, is the second solo album by the American guitarist and singer Joe Walsh. It was released on ABC-Dunhill Records and became his commercial breakthrough, thanks above all to the hit Rocky Mountain Way, which reached the top forty. The album even entered the top ten.

He shares the singing and writing with the other members of Barnstorm: drummer Joe Vitale, bassist Kenny Passarelli and newcomer Rocke Grace. As a result, you hear blues, jazz, folk, pop and even Caribbean music. Because the album was released under his name alone, the band fell apart. The cover shows a British First World War Sopwith Snipe. AllMusic calls each of the nine songs worthwhile.
werk/joe-walsh-the-smoker-you-drink-the-.listen: Listen to Rocky Mountain Way, the hit of the album, and notice the guitar.

werk/joe-zawinul-dialects.text:
Dialects, from 1986, is the fourth studio album by keyboardist Joe Zawinul, and it is almost a solo record. He made it himself, with programmed synthesizers and drum machines. He used vocoders on his own voice. In addition, Bobby McFerrin sang improvised vocal imitations, and a vocal trio sang in a language Zawinul had invented himself. He also did the production and design himself.

The record thus consists almost entirely of synthesizers and voices. A reviewer for Spin heard in the rhythms, harmonies and bop and funk arrangements a mixture of Prince and the young Miles Davis and Dizzy Gillespie. AllMusic called it an important, overlooked album, because it proves that electronic instruments can move and stir listeners when someone truly masters them.
werk/joe-zawinul-dialects.listen: Listen to The Harvest and try to hear what is a synthesizer and what is a voice. On this album that is surprisingly difficult.

werk/joe-zawinul-money-in-the-pocket.text:
Money in the Pocket is the first album under his own name by the jazz fusion keyboardist Joe Zawinul. It was released in 1966 on Atlantic and was the first of three albums he recorded for that label. He plays piano, with, among others, Blue Mitchell on trumpet, Joe Henderson on tenor saxophone and Pepper Adams on baritone saxophone.

The album sounds like an ordinary mix of hard bop and soul jazz from the mid-sixties. The Guardian pointed to the driving grooves, the many backbeats, repeated riffs and tight stops of the horns. All About Jazz found it remarkable that the record gives no hint yet of the great stylistic changes his work would undergo a few years later. AllMusic gave three stars.
werk/joe-zawinul-money-in-the-pocket.listen: Listen to the title track Money In the Pocket and notice the interplay of horns and rhythm section in this soul jazz.

werk/johann-johannsson-englaborn.text:
Englabörn is the first full studio album by the Icelandic musician Jóhann Jóhannsson, released in 2002 by Touch Music. He wrote the music for a play by Hávar Sigurjónsson. It was performed by a string quartet, percussionists and the composer himself, who plays several instruments, including piano, organ, harmonium and glockenspiel.

The album consists mainly of short pieces in which classical, ambient and electronic influences come together. It received glowing attention: Pitchfork gave it an 8.9 on release. A 2018 reissue on Deutsche Grammophon also contains reworks by other musicians, such as Ryuichi Sakamoto and Hildur Guðnadóttir.
werk/johann-johannsson-englaborn.listen: Listen to Englabörn and notice how the strings and the electronic sounds together create a single atmosphere.

werk/johann-johannsson-fordlandia.text:
Fordlândia is the sixth studio album by the Icelandic composer Jóhann Jóhannsson and was released on 3 November 2008 on 4AD, after IBM 1401, A User's Manual from 2006. The album revolves around the idea of a failed utopia. In the 1920s Henry Ford established a rubber plantation in the Amazon, complete with American small towns, hamburgers and prohibition. The Brazilian workers rebelled, and no rubber was ever produced for Ford's car tyres.

Jóhannsson wrote, arranged and produced everything himself. He plays piano, organ, guitar and electronics. The City of Prague Philharmonic Orchestra and Chorus plays on four tracks, and there are also strings, clarinet, pipe organ and percussion. The short Melodia pieces run through the record like a thread. Recording took place in Prague, Drammen and Reykjavík. Vaughan Oliver of v23 designed the cover.
werk/johann-johannsson-fordlandia.listen: Listen to How We Left Fordlandia, the longest track, and notice how the orchestra and the choir close the album here.

werk/johann-johannsson-vir-ulegu-forseta.text:
Virðulegu Forsetar, in Dutch Geachte voorzitters (roughly "Honourable Chairmen"), is the second studio album by Jóhann Jóhannsson, released in 2004 by Touch Music. It consists of a single ambient-influenced classical piece in which the same phrase keeps returning. For technical reasons it is divided into four parts.

The work was made for an ensemble conducted by Guðni Franzson, with The Caput Ensemble, wind instruments, organ, bass and electronics, while the composer himself played piano and electronics. After his death in 2018, his friend Adam Wiltzie organised a memorial concert at which the piece was performed, on the day he would have turned 49, in a church in Brussels.
werk/johann-johannsson-vir-ulegu-forseta.listen: Listen to Pt. 1.0 and notice which phrase returns and how the sound around it slowly changes.

werk/john-barry-thunderball.text:
Thunderball is the soundtrack album for the fourth James Bond film. John Barry wrote and conducted the music, and it was his third Bond score. United Artists released the album in 1965. Recording was still under way when the record had to be released, so the LP contained only twelve pieces from the first part of the film. The reason was a late change: the planned title song Mr. Kiss Kiss, Bang Bang by Barry and Leslie Bricusse was scrapped, because the studio wanted the song to name the title of the film.

The composer wrote Thunderball in a hurry with lyricist Don Black. Tom Jones sang it and, according to the stories, fainted after the high final note. Parts of the old melody remained in the score, for example in Cafe Martinique and as a bongo cha-cha-cha in Death of Fiona. The underwater motif from Search for Vulcan also runs through the film. An expanded CD edition followed in 2003.
werk/john-barry-thunderball.listen: Listen to Death of Fiona and notice the bongos and the fast cha-cha-cha. It is the melody of the discarded Mr. Kiss Kiss Bang Bang, here in a very different guise.

werk/john-cale-church-of-anthrax.text:
This is a collaboration between John Cale and Terry Riley. They recorded the album in the spring of 1969, but it was not released until February 1971, on CBS. Riley had just had success with A Rainbow in Curved Air, and Cale was coming from his influential work with The Velvet Underground. Most of it was improvised on the spot, with two drummers, Bobby Gregg and Bobby Colomby. The sound blends Riley's drones and patterns with free jazz and experimental rock. The Soul of Patrick Lee is the only track with vocals. The two disagreed about the end result: Cale laid extra guitar tracks over the recordings, and Riley therefore stayed away from the final mixing session.

The reception was mixed. Rolling Stone called it one of the best records of the year, but it was largely ignored. After the 2014 reissue the verdict was milder.
werk/john-cale-church-of-anthrax.listen: Listen to Church of Anthrax and notice how Cale's viola and bass and Riley's organ and saxophone together form a dense, swirling sound. Try to pick out the individual instruments.

werk/john-cale-fear.text:
Fear is John Cale's fourth solo album and was released on 1 October 1974 on Island Records. It is the first of three studio albums for Island, released within little more than a year. In the meantime Cale also produced records for others, such as Patti Smith's Horses. He sings and plays keyboards, guitars, viola, violin and bass. Guests include Richard Thompson of Fairport Convention and Brian Eno and Phil Manzanera of Roxy Music.

In Gun, Manzanera and Eno play an unusual guitar solo together: Eno processes Manzanera's guitar playing with a synthesizer as he plays. According to Crawdaddy, the album is a patchwork of Cale's past, with short, clear melodies and a sparer sound than the exuberant orchestration of the previous record. Trouser Press called it a brilliant record full of surprises and unsettling songs. The Man Who Couldn't Afford to Orgy was released as a single.
werk/john-cale-fear.listen: Listen to Gun and notice the guitar solo, in which Manzanera's playing is processed by Eno's synthesizer.

werk/john-cale-paris-1919.text:
The Welsh musician John Cale recorded his third solo album in 1972 and 1973 at Sunwest in Los Angeles, with producer Chris Thomas, who had previously worked with Procol Harum. He brought in Thomas for more objectivity in the recording process. Members of Little Feat played on it, including Lowell George and Richie Hayward, together with Wilton Felder and the University of California, Los Angeles symphony orchestra.

Where much of his work is experimental, this album sounds orchestral and accessible, in the spirit of Brian Wilson, the Bee Gees and Procol Harum. The title refers to the Paris Peace Conference of 1919, and the lyrics deal with European culture and history of the early twentieth century. Half Past France is, according to him, about soldiers who are already dead. The album was warmly received and is regarded as his best-known solo album.
werk/john-cale-paris-1919.listen: In Half Past France, listen to the lyrics: according to the singer, soldiers who are already dead talk in it about what has happened.

werk/john-cale-the-academy-in-peril.text:
The Academy in Peril is the second solo album by the Welsh musician John Cale and was released on 19 July 1972 on Reprise Records. Like his previous record, Church of Anthrax with Terry Riley, it is largely instrumental. The title refers to Cale's classical training, and you can hear that in the pieces. Cale himself plays bass, guitar, keyboards and viola. Adam Miller sings, Del Newman plays drums and Ron Wood plays slide guitar on The Philosopher.

In Legs Larry at Television Centre, Legs Larry Smith reads a text aloud. The Royal Philharmonic Orchestra plays on 3 Orchestral Pieces and on John Milton. Andy Warhol conceived and made the cover. The song Days of Steam was released as a single in New Zealand. AllMusic later wrote that the record strikes an unexpectedly pleasing and often engrossing balance between classical and rock, without the worst hybrids of the time.
werk/john-cale-the-academy-in-peril.listen: Listen to Legs Larry at Television Centre and notice how the spoken text relates to the music beneath it.

werk/john-cale-vintage-violence.text:
After his years with The Velvet Underground, John Cale began a solo career in 1970. Vintage Violence cost only 15,000 dollars and was produced by Cale himself together with Lewis Merenstein. He assembled a band for it called Penguin, but it broke up as soon as the recording was finished. The music is far more accessible than his avant-garde past would have suggested: short, melodic songs. He himself later found the songs simple and not very original. On the cover he wears a glass mask over a nylon stocking, which he later saw as a symbol for the record: you do not really see the personality.

The reviews were mostly positive. Ed Ward in Rolling Stone compared the sound to a Byrds album produced by Phil Spector, and Greil Marcus placed it alongside Van Morrison's Astral Weeks, because of its intense personal vision.
werk/john-cale-vintage-violence.listen: Listen to Amsterdam and notice the mood: does this song fit the image you might have of an avant-gardist from the Velvet Underground?

werk/john-coltrane-a-love-supreme.text:
John Coltrane recorded A Love Supreme in a single session, on 9 December 1964, at Van Gelder Studio in Englewood Cliffs. He played with his quartet: pianist McCoy Tyner, bassist Jimmy Garrison and drummer Elvin Jones. Impulse! released the record in January 1965. It is a through-composed suite in four parts: Acknowledgement, Resolution, Pursuance and Psalm. Coltrane plays tenor saxophone throughout.

The first part begins with the stroke of a gong and cymbal work. Garrison then plays a four-note motif on double bass, on which Coltrane varies. That motif becomes the chanted words a love supreme, with Coltrane accompanying himself through overdubs. In Psalm he performs a poem from the liner notes without words, on saxophone. The record is regarded as a work of deep spirituality, was nominated for a Grammy in 1966 and is Coltrane's best-loved album. By around 1970 about 500,000 copies had been sold, far more than his usual print run.
werk/john-coltrane-a-love-supreme.listen: Listen to the beginning of Acknowledgement and notice the four-note motif on the double bass, and hear how it returns later as the chanted words a love supreme.

werk/john-coltrane-ascension.text:
Ascension was recorded without rehearsal on 28 June 1965 at Van Gelder Studio in Englewood Cliffs and was released in February 1966 on Impulse!. John Coltrane was then one of the most successful jazz musicians in the world, just after A Love Supreme. He expanded his quartet with younger players from the avant-garde, including Pharoah Sanders, Archie Shepp and Freddie Hubbard. Coltrane handed out lead sheets at the start, and much was devised on the spot. The group recorded two versions of roughly equal length: Edition I and Edition II.

The piece lasts about forty minutes without a break. Collective improvisations alternate with solos. The sound is dense and turbulent: seven horn players play at once and the lines merge into a field of sound. The album is regarded as a watershed in Coltrane's work. What came before was more conventional, what came after was looser and closer to free jazz. AllMusic called it the recording that placed him firmly in the avant-garde.
werk/john-coltrane-ascension.listen: Listen to Ascension, Edition I, Pt. 1 and notice how many horns play at the same time. Try to follow individual lines and hear how they flow together.

werk/john-coltrane-blue-train.text:
Blue Train is the only record John Coltrane made as a leader for Blue Note. Rudy Van Gelder recorded it on 15 September 1957 at his studio in Hackensack, New Jersey, right in the period when Coltrane was playing with Thelonious Monk's quartet at the Five Spot. Unlike his previous label, Blue Note paid the musicians to rehearse. Besides the saxophonist, Lee Morgan, Curtis Fuller, Kenny Drew, Paul Chambers and Philly Joe Jones played.

He wrote four of the five pieces himself, which was rare at the time. The album stays within hard bop, but his playing already points ahead: his solos are more harmonically constructed, with broken chords and a sense of timing that often lies just behind or ahead of the beat. In 1960 he called it his favourite album to that point. Michael Cuscuna, who produced the reissues for Blue Note, heard a floating, almost ghostly quality in the title track.
werk/john-coltrane-blue-train.listen: In Blue Train, listen to the blues theme and to how Coltrane plays long, broken chord lines in his solo that often land just off the beat.

werk/john-coltrane-giant-steps.text:
The contract John Coltrane signed with Atlantic in 1959 was arranged by Miles Davis's manager. A first session in March did not satisfy him, so it was not used. The actual recordings followed on 4 and 5 May, two weeks after he took part in the last session for Kind of Blue. Naima followed only in December, with the rhythm section of Davis's quintet.

On this album the saxophonist concentrated on chord changes that are each a major third apart, later called Coltrane changes. His fast, dense phrasing was known as sheets of sound. The title track is famous for its difficult chord sequence and became a practice piece for jazz musicians, a gateway to modern improvisation. Cousin Mary, Syeeda's Song Flute, Naima and Mr. P.C. are named after people in his circle. Naima and the title track became jazz standards. The album is regarded as one of the most influential jazz records and entered the National Recording Registry in 2004.
werk/john-coltrane-giant-steps.listen: In Giant Steps, listen to the saxophone solo: notice how fast the notes go by while the chords keep shifting key. Then compare that with the calmer melody of Naima.

werk/john-coltrane-interstellar-space.text:
Interstellar Space is a duo suite for saxophone and drums by John Coltrane and Rashied Ali. They recorded it on 22 February 1967 at Van Gelder Studio, the year in which Coltrane died. Impulse! Records released it in September 1974. It was barely planned: Ali came for an ordinary session and found only Coltrane there. Asked what they would play, Coltrane replied that it could be anything Ali wanted. They recorded the album in one go.

The original release had four tracks: Mars, Venus, Jupiter and Saturn. The melody of Venus also returns on another recording from that period. Rolling Stone called the record astonishing, and Robert Christgau wrote that the duets only come alive when you listen to them attentively. Other critics found the music hard to approach, but emotionally powerful.
werk/john-coltrane-interstellar-space.listen: Listen to Mars and notice how saxophone and drums, without bass or piano, keep responding to each other.

werk/john-coltrane-soultrane.text:
Soultrane was released in 1958 on Prestige. John Coltrane recorded it at Rudy Van Gelder's studio in Hackensack, New Jersey, three days after a session for Miles Davis at Columbia. He plays tenor saxophone, with Red Garland on piano, Paul Chambers on bass and Art Taylor on drums. None of the five tracks is his own.

The album shows his style of the late fifties, which the critic Ira Gitler called sheets of sound in the liner notes. It includes a long version of I Want to Talk About You, the Billy Eckstine ballad, which he would often play again later. Also on it are Good Bait by Tadd Dameron and Theme for Ernie. The album closes with an exceptionally fast version of Russian Lullaby. Producer Bob Weinstock related that he jokingly called the piece Rushin' Lullaby. The title comes from a 1956 album by Tadd Dameron.
werk/john-coltrane-soultrane.listen: In I Want to Talk About You, listen to the tenor saxophone in this long ballad. Then compare Russian Lullaby and notice the difference in tempo.

werk/john-denver-take-me-to-tomorrow.text:
Take Me to Tomorrow is John Denver's second studio album and was released in May 1970. The magazine Record World predicted that the single Follow Me would make him a hitmaker, and Cash Box called it a fine ballad. The album spent two weeks on the Billboard Top LP's and got no higher than number 197.

Anyone expecting the sweet folk music and the wise children's lyrics of later years will be disappointed. According to Allmusic, the album sounds firmly like folk rock, with lyrics that even include burping and latrines. There are two songs by Tom Paxton, including Forest Lawn, a dry jab at the funeral industry. Aspenglow is the song that often appears on compilations. According to the liner notes, the record together with Rhymes & Reasons forms a concert from 1969, of which this is the spicier second half.
werk/john-denver-take-me-to-tomorrow.listen: Listen to Forest Lawn and notice the dry humour with which the funeral industry is mocked.

werk/john-denver-whose-garden-was-this.text:
Whose Garden Was This is John Denver's third studio album. It was released in October 1970 and consists largely of covers. The track list includes The Night They Drove Old Dixie Down, Mr. Bojangles and Eleanor Rigby, and at the end also Jingle Bells.

The title song is by Tom Paxton. Vera Lynn recorded it in 1972 for her album Unforgettable Songs by Vera Lynn. She wanted to sing it on her BBC television programme, but found the song too short and asked Paxton for another verse. He wrote it, with the forest and the squirrels, and later often sang that longer version in his concerts. The tracks from the album later reappeared as bonus tracks on reissues of the albums John Denver and Spirit.
werk/john-denver-whose-garden-was-this.listen: Listen to Whose Garden Was This and notice how short and simple the song is.

werk/john-fogerty-centerfield.text:
After the quarrels with his record company, Fogerty had made no record for nine years, and he never released his album Hoodoo. In 1985 he returned with Centerfield, which he played entirely himself: he recorded every instrument single-handedly with overdubs. The cover shows a worn baseball glove, as in the title song.

The singles The Old Man Down the Road, Rock and Roll Girls and Centerfield became hits; the first was his only top ten hit as a solo artist. The album also had a legal sequel. Zanz Kant Danz became Vanz Kant Danz, to avoid a lawsuit from Saul Zaentz. Zaentz also sued Fogerty because The Old Man Down the Road was said to resemble a Creedence song, but Fogerty won. Spin wrote that his skills were intact.
werk/john-fogerty-centerfield.listen: Listen to Centerfield and notice the lyrics: how does Fogerty turn baseball into an image for his own comeback?

werk/john-fogerty-eye-of-the-zombie.text:
In September 1986 Fogerty's fourth solo album was released, and the first on which he played with a backing band. On the cover he wears a mask, made by make-up artist John Carl Buechler. Fogerty first wanted to have himself painted with tribal markings, but Warner Bros. refused, because David Lee Roth had already done so.

Change in the Weather leans on the Creedence sound, while Wasn't That a Woman and Soda Pop are his first excursions into funk and R&B of the sixties and seventies. The title song made the Billboard charts. Critics were divided: the record sold modestly and yet received a Grammy nomination, and SPIN spoke of his strongest and most passionate record.
werk/john-fogerty-eye-of-the-zombie.listen: Listen to Change in the Weather and notice the swampy, dark atmosphere: why would anyone mistake this for a Creedence song?

werk/john-fogerty-john-fogerty.text:
After his solo debut The Blue Ridge Rangers in 1973, John Fogerty released his second solo album in 1975. In the United States it came out on Asylum Records, internationally on Fantasy Records. As on the Creedence Clearwater Revival records, there is a mixture of original songs and covers. The title is simple, but he calls the album Old Shep, after his dog Shep, who appears with him on the cover.

Two songs from this album were made famous worldwide by other artists. Rockin' All Over the World became one of Status Quo's best-known songs in 1977. Dave Edmunds recorded Almost Saturday Night, and it became a fixture in his repertoire. The covers include Lonely Teardrops and Sea Cruise. In 2021 the record was reissued on CD and streaming via BMG, for the first time in North America since the late seventies.
werk/john-fogerty-john-fogerty.listen: Listen to Rockin' All Over the World and notice the vocals and the rhythm. Do you recognise the Status Quo version in it, if you know that one?

werk/john-lennon-imagine.text:
After the bare, small-scale setting of his first solo album, John Lennon opted for a richer sound in 1971. He recorded at his own Ascot Sound Studios, at EMI and at the Record Plant in New York, with Yoko Ono and Phil Spector as producers. His former Beatles colleague George Harrison, pianist Nicky Hopkins, bassist Klaus Voormann and drummers Alan White and Jim Keltner played on it. Later additions were strings and saxophone from King Curtis.

The title song is a plea for world peace and became his best-known song. How Do You Sleep? is an attack on Paul McCartney, written in a period of bad relations after the break-up of the Beatles. Oh My Love and How? come from his experiences with primal therapy. The album went to number one in the United States and the United Kingdom. According to AllMusic it is a beautiful collection of songs, even though it has less thematic range than its predecessor.
werk/john-lennon-imagine.listen: Listen to Jealous Guy and notice how the song is built around a simple melody. It originated as early as 1968 in India under the name Child of Nature.

werk/john-lennon-john-lennon-plastic-ono.text:
After the break-up of the Beatles in April 1970, John Lennon underwent primal therapy with Yoko Ono under Arthur Janov, first for four weeks in London and then for four months in Los Angeles. In this therapy you relive old childhood pain. It gave him the material for this album. The recording took place in September and October 1970 at Abbey Road, with Ringo Starr on drums and Klaus Voormann on bass. Lennon, Ono and Phil Spector produced together.

The sound is raw and spare, the lyrics are deeply personal. Mother is about abandonment by his parents, Working Class Hero about the way young people are turned into soldiers. In God he lists, over a piano climax, things he does not believe in, from Jesus and Hitler to Beatles. On release the reactions were mixed. Later the album grew into one of his best solo records.
werk/john-lennon-john-lennon-plastic-ono.listen: In God, listen to the list of things he does not believe in and to the ending, where he says he believes only in himself and Yoko.

werk/john-lennon-some-time-in-new-york-c.text:
In September 1971 John Lennon and Yoko Ono moved to New York, where they soon got involved in politics. They performed at a rally for the imprisoned John Sinclair and spoke out on the uprising at Attica prison and on the oppression of women. Between December 1971 and March 1972 they recorded the studio part of this double album with Phil Spector as co-producer. The American band Elephant's Memory backed them. The second record contains live recordings from London and New York, including with Frank Zappa and his band.

The lyrics are pamphlets in song form about sexism, imprisonment, colonialism and racism. The cover resembles a newspaper. On release the album received devastating reviews and sold modestly: in the United States it reached number 48. He was dismayed by the failure and recorded no new music for almost a year afterwards.
werk/john-lennon-some-time-in-new-york-c.listen: Listen to Attica State and notice how a political subject stands directly in the lyrics. Compare that with Sunday Bloody Sunday, which is about Northern Ireland.

werk/john-lennon-unfinished-music-no-1-t.text:
Unfinished Music No. 1: Two Virgins is the debut of John Lennon and Yoko Ono as a duo, and the first of three experimental albums on Apple Records. It came about in a single night in Lennon's home studio in Kenwood, while his wife Cynthia was on holiday in Greece. The recordings consist mainly of tape loops, while he tries out various instruments and sound effects and Ono sings freely over them.

Better known than the music is the cover, which shows the couple naked. EMI refused to distribute the album, so it went into the shops in a brown paper bag, via Track in the United Kingdom and Tetragrammaton in the United States. Critics and public wanted nothing to do with it. In the US it reached number 124; in the United Kingdom it did not chart.
werk/john-lennon-unfinished-music-no-1-t.listen: Listen to Two Virgins: Side One and notice the tape loops, the sound effects and Yoko Ono's voice.

werk/john-lennon-unfinished-music-no-2-l.text:
Unfinished Music No. 2: Life With the Lions was released in May 1969 on Zapple, a sub-label of Apple. It is the second of three experimental albums that John Lennon made with Yoko Ono, after the controversial Unfinished Music No. 1: Two Virgins. The series was meant to be an account of their life together.

The first side is a live recording from Cambridge of 2 March 1969: Ono screams and sings, Lennon plays loud, distorted guitar feedback. It was the first time a Beatle had performed without the rest of the band. The couple recorded the second side in their room at Queen Charlotte's Hospital in London. In No Bed for Beatle John they sing newspaper clippings about themselves. Baby's Heartbeat is a loop of the heartbeat of their unborn child, and Two Minutes Silence is silent, as a tribute to John Cage's 4'33".
werk/john-lennon-unfinished-music-no-2-l.listen: Listen to Two Minutes Silence and notice what you hear when nothing is being played: the room, your own surroundings, your own expectation.

werk/john-mayall-back-to-the-roots.text:
Back to the Roots is a double album from 1971 on Polydor. The recording took place in California and London. John Mayall invited former members of his band, including the guitarists Eric Clapton and Mick Taylor. Also playing are Harvey Mandel and Jerry McGee on guitar, Larry Taylor and Steven Thompson on bass, Keef Hartley and Paul Lagos on drums, Don Sugarcane Harris on violin and Johnny Almond on saxophone and flute. The bandleader sings himself and plays piano, harmonica and guitar. The USA Union line-up forms the core of the album.

In the late eighties he remixed a number of the tracks and released them together with older work as Archives to Eighties. An expanded CD version of Back to the Roots now contains both the original and the remixed tracks.
werk/john-mayall-back-to-the-roots.listen: In Devil's Tricks, at almost eight minutes the longest track on the album, listen to the role of the guitars.

werk/john-mayall-empty-rooms.text:
Empty Rooms was released in March 1970 on Polydor, as the follow-up to the live album The Turning Point, which had come out earlier that year. John Mayall played with the same musicians: Jon Mark on acoustic guitar, Johnny Almond on saxophones and flute and Stephen Thompson on bass. Mayall himself sang and played harmonica, guitars and keyboards, including a Moog synthesizer. There is no drummer, so the rhythm stays fluid and the sound is unusual, even for this bandleader. He wrote all the songs. They are mostly about his love for the photographer Nancy Throckmorton, to whom the record is dedicated.

On To a Princess, guest Larry Taylor, former bassist of Canned Heat, improvises a remarkable bass duet with Thompson. It is the only known studio record by this line-up, which broke up shortly after the recording. Taylor then joined Mayall's new band for USA Union.
werk/john-mayall-empty-rooms.listen: Listen to To a Princess and follow how two basses complement each other and play with each other, without a drummer.

werk/john-mayall-usa-union.text:
USA Union was released in 1970 on Polydor. The recording took place on 27 and 28 July of that year at Larrabee Studios in Los Angeles. John Mayall lived in Laurel Canyon in the late sixties and knew local musicians there. When his Turning Point band broke up, he had to form a new group quickly, because Polydor was asking for an album. He chose Harvey Mandel and Larry Taylor, who had just left Canned Heat, and violinist Don Sugarcane Harris.

The group worked without drums, as in the jazzy blues experiment of The Turning Point. He played guitar, piano and harmonica himself, Harris electric violin. Most of the songs are about his then love Nancy Throckmorton, who also took photographs for the cover. Nature's Disappearing, the opener, is about environmental problems. Leonard Feather wrote the liner notes.
werk/john-mayall-usa-union.listen: In Nature's Disappearing, listen to what the lyrics are about: it is the only song that is not about love.

werk/john-mclaughlin-devotion.text:
Devotion is guitarist John McLaughlin's second album and was released in 1970. He recorded it while he was a member of Tony Williams Lifetime. His bandmate Larry Young plays organ, Buddy Miles, drummer of Jimi Hendrix's Band of Gypsys, sits behind the drums and Billy Rich, bassist of Taj Mahal, plays bass. He was not satisfied with the production by Alan Douglas, who mixed the recordings while he was not there.

According to The Rolling Stone Jazz Record Guide, this is where the guitarist comes closest to ordinary rock playing. Rolling Stone called the record very good and as heavy as a Led Zeppelin fan could wish for. AllMusic calls it one of the best acid rock albums ever and an exception in his catalogue.
werk/john-mclaughlin-devotion.listen: In Devotion, the longest track, listen to McLaughlin's electric guitar and Larry Young's organ: how heavy and rock-like does this sound for a jazz guitarist?

werk/john-mclaughlin-extrapolation.text:
Extrapolation is guitarist John McLaughlin's debut. He recorded the album in January 1969 at Advision Studios in London. The producer was Giorgio Gomelsky, who also founded the label Marmalade Records on which the record was released later that year. Eddy Offord was the engineer. In the quartet, John Surman plays baritone and soprano saxophone, Brian Odgers double bass and Tony Oxley drums.

It was not until 1972 that the album was first released in the United States, when the guitarist was enjoying success as leader of the Mahavishnu Orchestra. It reached number 152 on the Billboard 200 there. Binky's Beam is dedicated to Binky McKenzie, a former jazz bassist.
werk/john-mclaughlin-extrapolation.listen: In Binky's Beam, listen to the interplay of electric guitar, saxophone, bass and drums in this small ensemble.

werk/johnny-cash-american-iv-the-man-com.text:
American IV is Johnny Cash's 67th studio album and the last to be released in his lifetime, on 5 November 2002. It is the fourth instalment of the American series, which many critics consider his best work of his final years. Rick Rubin produced. Cash was seriously ill and almost blind, and the recording was interrupted by hospital admissions.

Most of the songs are covers, which he plays in his own stripped-down way. For Personal Jesus, Rubin asked guitarist John Frusciante to make an acoustic version, which gave the song a bluesy feel. Hurt was written by Trent Reznor of Nine Inch Nails; he later said the song was no longer his. Guests such as Fiona Apple, Nick Cave and Don Henley sing along. The album was named Album of the Year at the 2003 CMA Awards and was Cash's first album in thirty years to go gold.
werk/johnny-cash-american-iv-the-man-com.listen: Listen to Hurt and notice how little sounds besides his voice and the acoustic accompaniment.

werk/johnny-cash-american-recordings.text:
Producer Rick Rubin saw Johnny Cash perform at the concert for Bob Dylan's thirtieth anniversary in late 1992 and felt that the music industry had wrongly written the singer off. He offered him a contract at his label, which was best known for rap and heavy metal, with plenty of creative freedom. So the singer recorded the first solo album of his career, without backing musicians, with only his guitar, in his cabin in Tennessee and at Rubin's home in Los Angeles.

It is a spare album of old songs and newly written numbers. Tom Waits supplied Down There By the Train, Glenn Danzig wrote Thirteen and Nick Lowe wrote The Beast in Me. Tennessee Stud and The Man Who Couldn't Cry were recorded live at the Viper Room in Los Angeles. The critical response was almost unanimously glowing, and the album won a Grammy. It marked the beginning of a new flowering for the singer.
werk/johnny-cash-american-recordings.listen: Listen to Down There By the Train, a gospel-style song of redemption written by Tom Waits, and notice how sparely it is delivered: one voice and an acoustic guitar.

werk/johnny-cash-johnny-cash-with-his-ho.text:
In 1955 Johnny Cash came to audition at Sun Records as a gospel singer. Owner Sam Phillips thought that was not commercially promising and sent him back to come up with a different sound. He returned with Hey Porter and Cry! Cry! Cry!, his first single in July 1955. On it he was accompanied by guitarist Luther Perkins and bassist Marshall Grant, whom Phillips called the Tennessee Two.

The album, which came out on 11 October 1957, was one of Sun's first LPs. It contains four singles: Cry! Cry! Cry!, Folsom Prison Blues, I Walk the Line and So Doggone Lonesome. Folsom Prison Blues reached the country chart's top five in early 1956. I Walk the Line spent six weeks at number one on the country chart and also entered the pop top twenty. Phillips produced, and later reissues added demos and alternate takes.
werk/johnny-cash-johnny-cash-with-his-ho.listen: In I Walk the Line, listen to the accompaniment of the Tennessee Two: Luther Perkins's guitar and Marshall Grant's bass.

werk/johnny-griffin-johnny-griffin-sexte.text:
Johnny Griffin Sextet was released in 1958 on Riverside and was the first album Johnny Griffin made there as a bandleader. It was recorded the day before the sessions for Way Out!. The tenor saxophonist plays here in a sextet with a rich line-up: Pepper Adams on baritone saxophone, Donald Byrd on trumpet, Kenny Drew on piano, Wilbur Ware on bass and Philly Joe Jones on drums.

The album contains five tracks of between six and almost ten minutes. Wilbur Campbell wrote Stix' Trix, and What's New? is a well-known song by Bob Haggart and Johnny Burke. Dizzy Gillespie wrote Woody 'n' You, and only on that track are the baritone saxophone and the trumpet absent. John Hines contributed Johnny G.G., and Griffin himself wrote Catharsis.
werk/johnny-griffin-johnny-griffin-sexte.listen: Listen to Woody 'n' You, the only track without Pepper Adams and Donald Byrd, and notice how the line-up sounds smaller there.

werk/johnny-griffin-the-congregation.text:
Johnny Griffin recorded The Congregation on 23 October 1957 and it was released the following year on Blue Note. It was his last recording for that label. The tenor saxophonist works here with a quartet: Sonny Clark on piano, Paul Chambers on bass and Kenny Dennis on drums. Alfred Lion produced the record and Rudy Van Gelder recorded it.

The cover was made by Reid Miles, with an illustration by Andy Warhol. The album contains six tracks, including the title song, Latin Quarter, Main Spring and the standards I'm Glad There Is You, It's You or No One and I Remember You. Scott Yanow wrote on AllMusic that Griffin is heard here in top form on an almost classic quartet record and that the record is recommended to lovers of bop.
werk/johnny-griffin-the-congregation.listen: Listen to I Remember You and notice how Griffin's tenor saxophone interprets the song, accompanied by piano, bass and drums.

werk/johnny-hodges-creamy.text:
Alto saxophonist Johnny Hodges recorded this album in 1955 for the Norgran label. He plays it with men from Duke Ellington's orchestra, the ensemble with which he made his name. Among them are Clark Terry, Lawrence Brown, Harry Carney and Sonny Greer, and Billy Strayhorn is at the piano.

The record is above all a relaxed session. The first side consists of a ballad medley of over a quarter of an hour, with old standards such as Whispering, Tenderly, Prelude to a Kiss and Polka Dots and Moonbeams. Then come longer pieces such as Scufflin, Honey Bunny and No Use Kicking, and two compositions by Strayhorn, Passion and Pretty Little Girl. AllMusic's review gave four out of five stars and felt that there are no surprises on it, but that the album is worth buying.
werk/johnny-hodges-creamy.listen: Listen to Tenderly and notice how the alto saxophone lets the melody unfold unhurriedly, with the band softly around it.

werk/johnny-hodges-duke-s-in-bed.text:
In 1956 alto saxophonist Johnny Hodges recorded this album for the Verve label. He had men from Duke Ellington's orchestra around him, among them trumpeters Clark Terry and Ray Nance, trombonist Quentin Jackson and baritone saxophonist Harry Carney. All the arrangements were written by Billy Strayhorn, who also plays piano.

The record consists of nine tracks, partly by Hodges himself and partly by Ellington and Strayhorn. Besides the title song there are well-known pieces such as Black and Tan Fantasy, Just Squeeze Me and Take the "a" Train, which at well over eight minutes is the longest track. Nance also plays violin and sings along. AllMusic gave the album three stars.
werk/johnny-hodges-duke-s-in-bed.listen: Listen to Take the "a" Train, which Strayhorn wrote himself, and notice how the alto saxophone plays together with the rest of the band.

werk/johnny-hodges-ellingtonia-56.text:
Ellingtonia '56 was recorded in 1956 by alto saxophonist Johnny Hodges and released on the Norgran label. The saxophonist had played in Duke Ellington's orchestra for years, and for this record he brought members of that orchestra into the studio. Billy Strayhorn plays piano, Jimmy Woode bass and Sam Woodyard drums. On some of the tracks the trumpeters Cat Anderson, Willie Cook and Clark Terry and the trombonists Quentin Jackson, John Sanders and Britt Woodman also play.

Almost all the pieces come from the leader himself or from people in the orchestra's circle. Strayhorn wrote Snibor and wrote Hi'Ya together with the saxophonist. Anderson wrote Night Walk and The Happy One. AllMusic gave the record three stars.
werk/johnny-hodges-ellingtonia-56.listen: Listen to Texas Blues, at almost twelve minutes the longest track. Notice how the alto saxophone is given room.

werk/johnny-hodges-the-big-sound.text:
The Big Sound was recorded in 1957 by Johnny Hodges, who played in Duke Ellington's orchestra, and was released on Verve. Many members of Ellington's orchestra play on the record, including Harry Carney, Paul Gonsalves, Clark Terry, Ray Nance and Billy Strayhorn on piano. Some of the pieces come from trumpeter Cat Anderson, others from the saxophonist himself, Mercer Ellington, Strayhorn and Terry.

It is not a record by Ellington himself, but the band sounds like an established unit rather than a loose studio orchestra. Bob Rusch wrote in his review for AllMusic that the orchestra, with its solid backing and an occasional solo, contributed to the beautiful pieces for the saxophonist. He called it great work by Hodges and fine work by Ellington. Little Rabbit Blues lasts almost ten minutes.
werk/johnny-hodges-the-big-sound.listen: Listen to Little Rabbit Blues, the longest track. Notice how the alto saxophone and the band alternate.

werk/jon-batiste-the-process.text:
The Process, from 2014, was made by a trio: pianist Jon Batiste, drummer Chad Smith of the Red Hot Chili Peppers and bassist and producer Bill Laswell. They recorded the album in 2013 as film music for a film that had yet to be written and that never materialised.

The pianist also plays electric piano, Hammond organ, electronic keyboards and percussion. Laswell provides bass, guitar and electronics, and Smith drums and percussion. The trio received guests. Tunde Adebimpe of TV on the Radio sings on Drop Away, rapper Killah Priest on Turn On the Light / Ascent and Toshinori Kondo plays trumpet on Haunted. The saxophonist and flautist Peter Apfelbaum can also be heard, including on The Drift. The tracks have titles such as B1, B2 and B3, and between those short titles are the longer pieces.
werk/jon-batiste-the-process.listen: Listen to Haunted and notice Toshinori Kondo's trumpet and how it relates to the rest of the trio.

werk/jon-lord-sarabande.text:
Sarabande is Jon Lord's second solo album. It was recorded from 3 to 6 September 1975 at the Stadthalle in Oer-Erkenschwick, near Düsseldorf, with Dieter Dierks's mobile studio. The Philharmonia Hungarica played under the direction of Eberhard Schoener. The composer played Hammond organ, piano, clavinet and synthesizers, and was joined by, among others, guitarist Andy Summers and drummer Pete York. Martin Birch mixed the recordings in Munich and produced the record together with him.

The suite has eight parts, with titles such as Fantasia, Gigue and Pavane. In Finale, the parade of themes on the record was made with tape loops. The cover shows an ouroboros, a snake biting its own tail, with three naked women on it. Not until 2010 was the whole suite performed live, in Budapest, with new orchestrations.
werk/jon-lord-sarabande.listen: In Finale, listen to the parade of themes and try to hear which earlier pieces return.

werk/joni-mitchell-blue.text:
After the success of Ladies of the Canyon, 1970 was a turbulent year for Joni Mitchell. Her relationship with Graham Nash was over, she had made a trip through Greece and Europe, and then an intense affair with James Taylor began. The material for Blue came from that time, recorded in late 1970 and early 1971 at A&M Studios in Hollywood. She wrote and produced everything herself. Many songs originated on the Appalachian dulcimer, an instrument she had come to know at a folk festival in 1969.

The accompaniment is sparse: acoustic guitar, piano and dulcimer, supplemented here and there by Taylor and Stephen Stills. Carey, inspired by a man she met in Greece, was the first single. The songs look sideways at love and loss, although she herself rejected the label confessional. Blue was a success on release and is now seen as her high point, with great influence on the singer-songwriters who came after her.
werk/joni-mitchell-blue.listen: Listen to Little Green and notice how little lies beneath the voice: mainly guitar, so that every word can be heard clearly.

werk/joni-mitchell-clouds.text:
Clouds is Joni Mitchell's second album and was released on 1 May 1969 on Reprise Records. Her debut Song to a Seagull had already made her better known, partly because other singers recorded her songs. For Clouds she went to A&M Studios in Hollywood. She produced almost everything herself and also painted the cover, a self-portrait. Stephen Stills plays guitar on it.

The sound consists mainly of her voice and acoustic accompaniment, with subtle, unusual harmonies, especially in Songs to Aging Children Come. Chelsea Morning and Both Sides, Now had already been recorded by others. She wrote Both Sides, Now after reading a novel by Saul Bellow in which someone looks at clouds from an aeroplane. The record received mostly good reviews and won a Grammy for Best Folk Performance. AllMusic found her voice more confident than on the debut.
werk/joni-mitchell-clouds.listen: Listen to Both Sides, Now and notice how voice and acoustic accompaniment together carry the image of the clouds, seen from two sides.

werk/joni-mitchell-court-and-spark.text:
In 1973 Joni Mitchell, for the first time in her career, released no album. After For the Roses she wanted to set aside a whole year for a new record in which her growing interest in jazz would be audible. Together with engineer Henry Lewy she brought top musicians from Los Angeles into the studio, including members of the Crusaders and of Tom Scott's L.A. Express. Robbie Robertson, David Crosby and Graham Nash dropped by, and Cheech & Chong provided a touch of comedy.

The result combines folk rock with jazz elements. Help Me became her only top 10 single on the American Hot 100. The album was released in January 1974, was an immediate success and is still her best-selling. The Village Voice named it best album of the year.
werk/joni-mitchell-court-and-spark.listen: Listen to Help Me and notice how a song with a jazzy sound could still work as a pop single, with Mitchell's voice and guitar in front.

werk/joni-mitchell-don-juan-s-reckless-d.text:
Don Juan's Reckless Daughter was released on 13 December 1977 on Asylum Records. It is a double album, the ninth by Joni Mitchell. Her contract with the label was nearly up, and according to her she therefore made this record looser than anything she had done before. The sound goes still further into jazz than on her earlier albums. Jazz musicians play on it, including four members of Weather Report: Jaco Pastorius, Wayne Shorter, Manolo Badrena and Alex Acuña.

Much of it is experimental. Overture opens with six guitars at once, some in different tunings. The Tenth World is a long instrumental composition with Latin percussion. Dreamland consists only of drums and voices, including Chaka Khan. Paprika Plains lasts sixteen minutes, with improvised piano and a full orchestra, and fills the whole second side. The reviews were mixed. Within three months the album was certified gold.
werk/joni-mitchell-don-juan-s-reckless-d.listen: In Paprika Plains, listen to how the piano and the orchestra together tell a story that lasts sixteen minutes, and notice how the music moves along with the singing.
